text: Traditional Celtic healing took several forms: herbal remedies, spells, and rituals. Modern biochemistry upholds some of the old plant remedies. Others stay untested or have proved ineffective. Many modern drugs come from plants. Aspirin, or salicylic acid, comes from willow, genus Salix, a known remedy against pain. In Scotland St. John's Wort, Hypericum pulchrum, kept away fairies who might steal people from their beds. This suggests that what we call depression was once described as fairy kidnapping. Other healing used magic. People attached trailing pearlwort, Sagina procumbens, to the skins of animals and people to guard against the evil eye. Such ritual may act through the placebo effect, in which people given sugar pills improve like patients given real medicine. In Ireland water from holy wells was sprinkled on or fed to the sick. In Scotland chanted spells mended sprains and boils. People visited places held sacred by pre-Celtic peoples, such as springs and stone circles. Thermal springs may ease arthritis by physical means. Most such sites have no detectable biological effect. Herb gathering often demanded ritual. The cutter used no iron, cut at set times, and was rewarded with wine. Ordinary people knew many of these cures. In hard cases they called local herbalists or witches, often older women who earned a living by advising their neighbors. Suspected of working ill, such a practitioner could be accused of witchcraft.
objective: Document the several forms and beliefs of traditional Celtic healing.
key_results: Record the herbal, spelled, and ritual methods of healing.
Describe the link to modern medicine and the placebo effect.
Note the holy wells, stone circles, and the herbalist and witch practitioners.
